article_title: Oracle's Notes Call JDK 21.0.13, Dated October 20, the First JDK 21 Update Under the OTN License, With a Next Update Listed for November 17
summary: Submission rejected as an Analysis: facts check out against the sources, but the Analysis requirements (independent sources that bear on the subject; examination of a topic rather than a recap of Oracle's own pages) are not met, and a mislabelled Analysis cannot be approved or relabelled.

findings.message: Independent coverage of the subject is absent: no editorial outlet in the source list reports on the JDK 21 licence change
findings.details: Of 15 cited URLs, 6 are Oracle pages (one outlet, the subject). Eclipse Temurin (2 GitHub release pages) and Amazon Corretto (changelog, 2 release pages, FAQ) are other vendors' own release notes, changelog and documentation for their own builds; none of the 6 pages mentions the Oracle licence change (0 hits for OTN/NFTC; the only licence text is the Corretto FAQ's statement of Corretto's own GPLv2+CPE licence). InfoQ (Oct 26 weekly roundup) mentions 21.0.13 in one sentence as part of Oracle's October CPU release list and says nothing about a licence (0 hits for licen/OTN/NFTC). The Register (Sept 7) is about the European Commission's interest in Oracle's licensing; it never mentions JDK 21, OTN or NFTC. The only independent text that discusses the change is one self-published DEV Community post (single author, Sept 25, written before the release, author states no hands-on migration experience), which is not an editorial outlet. Editorial outlets reporting on the change: 0. Outlets independent of Oracle by the letter of the policy: InfoQ and The Register (2), but neither says anything about the headline subject, so no claim in the headline, summary or lead is checked, corroborated or contextualised by anyone other than Oracle.

findings.message: The piece recaps Oracle's own pages around one release rather than examining a topic
findings.details: Overview states the piece 'reports what the cited pages say and does not interpret the license text'. Background, timeline, pricing and Implications restate Oracle's blog, FAQ, roadmap and release notes; the Implications section is quotation plus a restatement of the Nov 17 date. The 'Where the sources differ' bullets are small documentary discrepancies (a roadmap year, one blog post's phrase, CPU versus CSPU, Corretto timestamps), useful but not an examination of consequences, a trend or a real disagreement among sources. At 1,187 words it is also too long to stand as a Briefing (300-800), and it may not be relabelled.

findings.message: Every checked fact, quote, date, figure and version matches the raw sources; no headline, summary or lead error
findings.details: Verified item by item (see editor_notes.source_verification). Subordinate clarity points that would have been clarification records had the article been approved: (1) the Gartner estimate quoted from The Register concerns Oracle's January 2023 per-employee subscription model and predates the Oct 8, 2026 SMB prices it is placed beside; (2) the summary says the Herald 'compares' Oracle's pages with InfoQ, The Register, Temurin and Corretto, though none of those four discusses the licence change; (3) the build timeline omits the Oct 20 time-zone-only bundled patch release 21.0.13.0.1 listed in the same notes.

findings.message: Title is 139 characters (under the 150 limit), long but within bounds

content_preview.title: Oracle's Notes Call JDK 21.0.13, Dated October 20, the First JDK 21 Update Under the OTN License, With a Next Update Listed for November 17
content_preview.summary: Oracle's release notes mark JDK 21.0.13 as the first JDK 21 update under the Java SE OTN license instead of the NFTC; the Herald compares Oracle's pages with InfoQ, The Register, Temurin and Corretto.
content_preview.body_excerpt:
## Overview

Oracle's consolidated release notes describe [JDK 21.0.13](https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/21all-relnotes.html), dated October 20, 2026, as "the first JDK 21 update release made available under the Oracle Technology Network License Agreement for Oracle Java SE (OTN for Java SE)." The notes add that this license "is substantially different from the Oracle No-fee Terms and Conditions (NFTC) used in earlier JDK 21 updates." This analysis sets Oracle's own pages on the c...

Consider adding trusted domains to config/source_allowlist.txt

editor_notes.content_quality: Accurate, carefully hedged and neutral, 1,187 body words (inside the Analysis range of 800-2000). Structure is Overview, Background, Current situation, Where the sources differ, Implications. Facts and commentary are separated and there is no Herald prediction or opinion. The weakness is not accuracy but what kind of piece it is: a documentary digest of Oracle's pages about a single release and its surrounding announcements, with side information from other parties. The topic is also not strictly the last 10 days (the release is Oct 20; the latest dated item is Oct 24), noted only.

Route for the three blogs.oracle.com posts (live fetch with a browser User-Agent returns HTTP 403 'fw_error_www' today; the writer read them through web.archive.org): I read the Archive.org raw captures (id_ form) and compared the article body text with the stored snapshots: line-for-line identical for all three. CLAIMS CONFIRMED: Release notes (src 0): 21.0.13 'Release date: October 20, 2026', full version 21.0.13+10; 'JDK 21.0.13 is the first JDK 21 update release made available under the Oracle Technology Network License Agreement for Oracle Java SE (OTN for Java SE). This license is substantially different from the Oracle No-fee Terms and Conditions (NFTC) used in earlier JDK 21 updates.' verbatim; 21.0.13.0.2 'Release date: October 21, 2026' (eMudhra intermediates distrusted, CVE-2026-91403); 21.0.13.0.3 'Release date: October 24, 2026' (CVE-2026-114820); the three notes each say 'not recommended ... after the next critical patch update scheduled for November 17, 2026'; 21.0.12.1 'Release date: August 18, 2026' with the quoted 'update releases of Oracle JDK 21 after September of 2026 will switch to the Java SE OTN license' and 'Users wishing to receive updates ... should migrate to Oracle JDK 25'; 21.0.12 'Release date: July 21, 2026'; 21.0.13 'This release contains fixes for security vulnerabilities described in the Oracle Critical Patch Update.' Omitted by the article: 21.0.13.0.1 BPR (Oct 20, time-zone fixes). Blog Aug 14 (src 1): Donald Smith, Vice President of Product Management; all quoted phrases verbatim ('started the one-year transition period for NFTC users of JDK 21', 'all updates through and including September 2026 are available under the NFTC', 'beginning with the October 2026 Critical Patch Update (CPU), are planned to be offered under the Java SE OTN license', GraalVM OTN licence from the October 2026 CPU, the five user groups, 'remains available until at least September 2031', JDK 25 NFTC 'until October 2028' one year after Java 29). FAQ (src 2, 'Updated October 20, 2026'): Java 21 table rows 'releases after September 2026 (21.0.13 and later)' / OTN 'for Personal, Development and other Users only' and 'releases through September 2026 (21.0.12 and earlier)' / NFTC 'for All Users'; 'You may continue to use releases you have downloaded under the terms of the license under which you downloaded them'; JDK 25 'until September of 2028' one year after Java 29 (blog says October 2028; both reported, correct). Roadmap (src 3, 'Updated October 20, 2026'): 'Java SE 21 was released in September 2023 and public updates through September 2025 were under a permissive license' in the same paragraph as 'Oracle JDK 21 releases as of October 20, 2026, are available under the Java SE OTN license' and 'Oracle JDK 17, released as of October 15, 2024'; the 2025 versus 2026 conflict is real, the page offers no explanation, and the article reports it unreconciled as it should. Blog Sept 10 update (src 4): 'Oracle is currently planning a Java CSPU for November 17th, in addition to our regularly scheduled October and January CPU releases'; 'We plan to provide multiple monthly updates in CY27; organizations should be preparing for this cadence'. Blog Oct 8 (src 5): $100 / $1,000 / $10,000 / $147.20 per additional employee 501-2,999 'in addition to $10,000 for the first 500'; '3,000 Employees or more: Unchanged' (article's figures and scope exact; it omits the 'in addition to $10,000' qualifier but also states $10,000 for 500 or fewer). InfoQ (src 6, Michael Redlich, Oct 26 2026, roundup of Oct 19): 'Oracle has released versions 27.0.1 25.0.5, 21.0.13, 17.0.21, 11.0.33 and 8u511 ... as part of their quarterly Critical Patch Update Advisory for October 2026'; Azul October CPU for Zulu 27, 25, 21, 17, 11, 8, 7, 6 'covers 53 CVEs'; BellSoft CPU patches 21.0.12.1.1 and PSU 21.0.13; no mention of any licence, OTN or NFTC. WHAT INFOQ COVERS: a weekly Java news roundup; the 21.0.13 item is one sentence in a list. The Register (src 7, Lindsay Clark, Sept 7 2026): MLex-reported European Commission scrutiny of Oracle licensing after the SAP commitments; one paragraph on Java ('Oracle announced a new licensing regime for Oracle Java SE in January 2023 ...', 'Gartner estimated the per-employee subscription model to be two to five times more expensive than the legacy version' verbatim); no mention of JDK 21, OTN, NFTC or the 21.0.13 release (confirmed by grep). WHAT THE REGISTER COVERS: EU competition scrutiny of Oracle licensing generally, not the JDK 21 change. Temurin (src 8, 9): GitHub API published_at 2026-10-22T08:58:06Z (21.0.13+9) and 2026-08-19T12:10:19Z (21.0.12.1+1); release body is the single line 'Official Eclipse Temurin Release of jdk-21.0.13+9'; no CVE or licence text. Corretto (src 10-13): CHANGELOG 21.0.13.0.10 'Release Date: October 20, 2026', 'Import jdk-21.0.13+9 ... Updates Corretto baseline to OpenJDK 21.0.13+9'; 21.0.13.0.11 'Release Date: October 24, 2026', CVE-2026-114820 CVSS 9.1; GitHub published_at 2026-10-23T05:53:31Z and 2026-10-27T00:08:25Z (created_at 2026-10-23T08:13:10Z and 2026-10-24T21:39:16Z), nothing explains the gap and the article gives both; FAQ: 'licensed under the terms of the GNU Public License version 2 with the Class Path Exception (GPLv2 with CPE)', Corretto 21 'Last Planned Update: July 2030'. DEV Community (src 14, jamilxt, 'Posted on Sep 25'): '21.0.12 ... This is the last free-for-production JDK 21 build' with 'July 21, 2026'; the article cites it accurately; the post otherwise contains un-sourced and wrong-for-Oracle-pages statements (e.g. 'Production use requires a paid subscription', '$15 per employee per month') that the article correctly does not repeat. Quantifier and absence sweep (grep of title, summary, body): 'each say' (three notes) verified for all three; 'all updates through and including September 2026' is a quotation; 'The Herald has not covered the change before' verified against src/content/articles; no 'no source reports' sentences. Anthropic disclosure: not required - Anthropic is not named in the article and the topic is Oracle/OpenJDK licensing. Allowlist: www.oracle.com (host oracle.com after stripping www.) is not listed (only oracle.com/news and blogs.oracle.com); the script's warning is the only automated finding. Confirmation evidence for a future submission: the allowlisted blogs.oracle.com Java blog (Donald Smith, Oracle VP Product Management) links to https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/java-se-support-roadmap.html and https://www.oracle.com/java/technologies/javase/jdk-faqs.html as 'Oracle Java SE Support Roadmap' and 'Oracle Java SE Licensing FAQ', both pages carry '(c) 2026 Oracle' and the Oracle account/OCI navigation; I did not add the host because the article is rejected on other grounds. INDEPENDENT-SOURCE RECOUNT (per outlet): Oracle = 1 outlet (6 pages, the subject); Eclipse Temurin = 1 (other vendor's own release pages, no reporting on Oracle); Amazon Corretto = 1 (AWS's own changelog, release pages and FAQ, no reporting on Oracle); InfoQ = 1 editorial outlet, restates the CPU release list only; The Register = 1 editorial outlet, background on Oracle licensing generally; DEV Community = 1 individual's self-published post, the only text on the JDK 21 change. Editorial outlets reporting on the JDK 21 licence/update change = 0. Pattern scan: no suspicious_patterns, no text addressed to an AI agent found in any snapshot. Originality: no earlier Herald article on the OTN transition; the Nov 6 eMudhra article is linked correctly (/article/2026-11/06-emudhra-...).
editor_notes.factual_accuracy: No error found in the headline, summary or lead or in any subordinate claim: dates (Oct 20, 21, 24, Nov 17, Aug 14, 18, Sept 10, Oct 8), build numbers, figures and quotations all match the raw text of their sources; both Oracle-internal disagreements (roadmap 'through September 2025' versus September 2026 elsewhere; JDK 25 NFTC end 'October 2028' in the blog versus 'September of 2028' in the FAQ) and the Corretto changelog/GitHub timestamp gap exist as the article describes. The headline attributes the 'first JDK 21 update under OTN' to Oracle's notes and describes the licence terms exactly as Oracle words them, with no legal characterisation.
editor_notes.tone_assessment: Neutral and professional; attribution is careful ('Oracle's notes say'), no sensationalism, no AI self-reference, no Herald opinion or prediction.
editor_notes.originality: New topic for the Herald; no overlap with published articles (only the eMudhra article is referenced for continuity).
concerns: Analysis requirement on independence is not met in substance: no editorial outlet in the source list reports on the JDK 21 licence change. InfoQ is a one-sentence mention of the 21.0.13 release inside a weekly roundup; The Register (Sept 7) never mentions JDK 21; Temurin and Corretto are other vendors' own release pages and changelog that document their own builds and say nothing about Oracle's licence; the DEV Community item is one self-published pre-release post. All claims in the headline, summary and lead rest on Oracle's own pages alone.

Analysis requirement on topic is not met: the piece is a restatement of Oracle's blog, FAQ, roadmap and release notes around one release (it says itself that it 'does not interpret the license text'), and its Implications section adds no examination beyond quotation. It is also too long (1,187 words) to be a Briefing (300-800) and may not be relabelled.

Clarity points (would have been clarification records): Gartner estimate relates to the January 2023 model and is placed next to the Oct 8, 2026 prices; summary implies all four named non-Oracle sources are compared on the licence change; the 21.0.13.0.1 BPR is omitted from the build timeline.
recommendations: The facts in this submission are sound. If the topic is worth covering again, commission it as a Briefing of 800 words or fewer built on Oracle's release notes, FAQ and blog posts, or as an Analysis only after independent reporting on the JDK 21 licence change exists (trade press, analyst or licensing-advisor commentary) and the piece examines consequences or a real disagreement among those sources.
If resubmitted, www.oracle.com needs allowlisting under the confirmation procedure (evidence recorded in source_verification).
editor_notes.overall_assessment: Rejected as an Analysis: accurate and well hedged, but the independent sources do not bear on the subject and the article recaps Oracle's own pages around one release, so it does not meet the Analysis requirements and cannot be approved as one or relabelled. Featured candidacy: 0 - routine release-licence documentation for a defined audience; not published.
